It is only four o'clock, but this is winter, and the sun has already set. There are no clouds in the clear, freezing sky to reflect its slanting rays. Instead, the air itself has a faint pink glow, reflected again in the snow covering the ground. I live in an isolated cottage on a wide, lonely heath. No sound of life reaches me. The empty plain is white except for a few dark patches on the tops of the steep, pointed mounds. Snow slid from them as it fell, leaving a thinner layer than on the flat ground, and the midday sun has melted it away. A few birds peck at the hard ice over the pools, for the frost has lasted a long time.

My state of mind is strange. I am alone—utterly alone—in the world. Misfortune has swept over me and left me withered. I know I am going to die, and I feel happy, even joyful. I feel my pulse: it beats quickly. I put my thin hand to my cheek: it burns. A frail, restless spark of life inside me is giving off its last flashes. I will never see another winter's snow. I believe I will never again feel the life-giving warmth of a summer sun. With that certainty, I begin to write my tragic story. Perhaps a story like mine should die with me, but an unnamed feeling urges me on. My body and mind are too weak to resist even the slightest impulse. When I was strong, I thought my story contained a sacred horror that made it impossible to speak of. Now, as I approach death, I reveal and profane its mysterious terrors. It is like the grove of the Eumenides, which only the dying may enter—and Oedipus is about to die.

What am I writing? I must gather my thoughts. Perhaps nobody will read these pages except you, my friend, who will receive them after my death. Yet I will not write only to you. It will please me to describe our friendship in a way that would be unnecessary if you alone were my reader. So I will tell my story as though writing for strangers. You have often asked why I live alone, why I weep, and above all why I keep such an unkind, unbreakable silence. While living, I dared not answer. In death, I reveal the mystery. Others may glance carelessly through these pages. But to you, Woodville, my kind and loving friend, they will be precious reminders of a heartbroken girl who still feels gratitude towards you as she dies. Your tears will fall on the words describing my sorrows. I know they will, and while I still live, I thank you for your sympathy.

Rereading his letter while composing her answer had so softening an effect that a few firm expressions were especially needed to strengthen her resolution. She was so troubled by the prospect of causing him pain, so occupied with what his mother and sisters would say and think, and so eager not to appear ungrateful, that Emma believed she would have accepted the young man after all had he crossed her path at that instant.

Nevertheless, the letter was composed, sealed, and dispatched. The affair was concluded, and Harriet secured. She remained rather dispirited throughout the evening, but Emma could excuse her kindly regrets. Sometimes she eased them by declaring her own affection; at other times she introduced the thought of Mr. Elton.

“I shall never be asked to Abbey-Mill again,” Harriet said in a somewhat mournful voice.

“And if you were, my Harriet, I could never endure letting you go. Hartfield needs you far too much to spare you to Abbey-Mill.”

“I'm certain I should never wish to go, either, for nowhere but Hartfield makes me happy.”

A little later she said, “I think Mrs. Goddard would be greatly astonished if she knew what has happened. Miss Nash certainly would, because she considers her own sister so well married, and her husband is only a linen-draper.”

“One would be sorry to find more pride or refinement in a schoolteacher, Harriet. I daresay Miss Nash would envy you this chance of marriage. Even such a conquest would seem precious to her. As for anything better for you, she is surely quite unaware. A certain person's attentions can scarcely have reached the gossip of Highbury yet. So far, I fancy only you and I have understood what his looks and behaviour mean.”

Harriet smiled and coloured, and murmured something about her surprise that people should like her so well. Thinking of Mr. Elton was certainly a comfort; yet after a while her tenderness for the rejected Mr. Martin returned.

“He has my letter by now,” she said quietly. “I wonder what they are doing, and whether his sisters know. If he is miserable, they will be miserable as well. I hope he won't take it too much to heart.”

“Let us turn to those absent friends whose occupations are happier,” Emma exclaimed. “Perhaps at this very moment Mr. Elton is showing your portrait to his mother and sisters, explaining how much lovelier the original is, and, after they have asked him five or six times, finally permitting them to hear your name—your own dear name.”

“Will you play?”

“I believe, sir,” the spy said in a thoroughly servile manner, turning towards Mr. Lorry, “that I may appeal to a gentleman of your age and kindness. Ask this other gentleman, so much younger than yourself, whether playing the Ace he mentioned could ever be consistent with his position. I admit that I am a spy, and that the occupation is regarded as dishonorable, although someone has to fill it. But this gentleman is no spy. Why should he lower himself by becoming one?”

“I'll play my Ace, Mr. Barsad,” Carton answered for himself, checking his watch, “without the slightest hesitation, in a very few minutes.”

“I had hoped, gentlemen,” the spy said, still trying to draw Mr. Lorry into the discussion, “that your respect for my sister—”

“I could show my respect for your sister in no better way than by finally freeing her of her brother,” Sydney Carton said.

“You think so, sir?”

“My mind is quite made up.”

The spy's polished manner was oddly at odds with his conspicuously rough clothes and probably with his usual behavior. It faltered and deserted him under the pressure of Carton's unreadable expression. Carton had puzzled wiser and more honest men than this one. While the spy struggled for a response, Carton resumed his earlier air of studying a hand of cards.

“In fact, thinking it over, I have a strong feeling there's another good card here that I haven't yet counted. That friend and fellow Sheep who described himself as grazing in the provincial prisons—who was he?”

“A Frenchman. You don't know him,” the spy replied quickly.

“French, is he?” Carton repeated thoughtfully, seeming not to notice the man despite echoing his words. “Well, perhaps he is.”

“He is, I assure you,” said the spy, “though it doesn't matter.”

“Though it doesn't matter,” Carton repeated in the same automatic way. “Though it doesn't matter. No, it doesn't matter. No. Still, I know that face.”

“I don't think so. I'm certain you don't. It isn't possible,” said the spy.

“It—isn't—possible,” Sydney Carton murmured, searching his memory and toying again with his glass, which fortunately was small. “Not possible. Spoke good French. But like a foreigner, I thought?”

“A provincial accent,” the spy said.

“No. Foreign!” Carton exclaimed, slapping his open hand on the table as the answer came to him. “Cly! Disguised, but the same man. We saw him at the Old Bailey.”

“Now you're being hasty, sir,” Barsad replied, smiling so that his hooked nose seemed to lean farther to one side. “Now you've really given me an advantage.
